html:
Three Paths, One Very Expensive Decision

Most insurers we talk to already know their current policy administration setup is costing them money. The real question is which modernization path is least likely to blow up mid-implementation. That’s actually not a small distinction at all.

The short answer: there’s no universal winner between cloud-native rebuild, SaaS adoption, and hybrid migration. Each model suits a different risk tolerance, regulatory posture, and operational reality. What follows is a practical breakdown of all three, with enough specificity to actually inform a vendor or architecture decision. Not just validate one you’ve already made.

Why Policy Administration Is the Core of This Conversation

Policy administration sits at the center of everything an insurer does operationally. Rating, billing, claims triggering, endorsements, renewals, regulatory filings – all of it flows through the policy admin layer. When that layer is a 30-year-old COBOL system running on a mainframe, you don’t just have a technology problem. You have a talent problem (finding COBOL developers gets harder every single year), a speed-to-market problem, and a data problem, because getting clean structured data out of those systems is genuinely painful in ways that vendor presentations rarely capture.

According to the KPMG Insurance Technology Survey 2026, over 60% of insurers still rely on legacy core systems for at least part of their policy administration workflow, and the majority cite core modernization as their top-priority technology investment for the next two years. That tracks with what we see in practice. The appetite is real. The execution is where things get complicated.

The Three Delivery Models, Plainly Described

Cloud-Native Rebuild

This means building a new insurance policy management system from scratch using cloud-native architecture: microservices, APIs, containerized workloads, typically on AWS or Azure. You’re not migrating anything. You’re replacing it. The old system runs in parallel until the new one is ready, then you cut over.

The appeal is obvious enough. You get exactly the architecture you want, no legacy constraints, full ownership of the data model, and the ability to ship product changes fast once you’re live. AWS insurance industry benchmark data suggests that insurers running cloud-native policy administration systems can reduce time-to-market for new products by 40-60% compared to those still on legacy platforms – though that number assumes a reasonably mature DevOps practice, which not every carrier actually has.

The problem is cost and duration. A meaningful cloud-native rebuild for a mid-size insurer typically runs two to four years and eight figures in investment before you see production traffic on the new system. We’ve seen this fail when carriers underestimate the data migration and parallel-run period. Running two systems simultaneously isn’t cheap, and business users will exploit any ambiguity about which system is authoritative. They always do.

SaaS Platform Adoption

Here you’re subscribing to a vendor-managed insurance policy admin platform. Guidewire Cloud, Duck Creek On Demand, Majesco, and a few others are the main names in this space. The vendor handles infrastructure, upgrades, security patching, and often regulatory content libraries. You configure rather than build.

Speed is the main argument for SaaS. You can have a functioning system in 12 to 18 months for a defined line of business, sometimes faster. The vendor’s upgrade cadence means you’re not carrying technical debt the same way. And because these platforms have already gone through SOC 2, ISO 27001, and often state insurance regulatory scrutiny, your compliance posture is mostly inherited rather than built from scratch.

The trade-offs are real, though. SaaS means giving up some control. If the vendor’s data model doesn’t fit your product structures, you’re either customizing heavily (which erodes the upgrade benefits you paid for) or changing your products to fit the platform. Neither is a comfortable choice. Pricing is also opaque – most SaaS policy administration vendors charge on a per-policy or GWP-percentage basis, which can get expensive fast as you scale. Understand your exit costs before you sign anything.

Hybrid Lift-and-Shift

This is the path many carriers actually end up on, often by default rather than design. You move existing insurance policy administration systems to a cloud environment (typically IaaS, meaning Infrastructure as a Service) without fundamentally re-architecting them. The mainframe to cloud migration happens at the infrastructure level: the application logic stays largely intact, but now it runs on AWS EC2 instances or Azure VMs instead of dedicated hardware.

The benefit is speed and risk reduction in the short term. You get off aging hardware, reduce data center costs, and open the door to cloud-native tooling around your existing core. It’s also reversible, which matters to risk-averse organizations and their boards.

Here’s the honest caveat, though: this is often a way of deferring the real modernization rather than achieving it. You still have the same COBOL. You still have the same data model. You’ve just moved the problem to a different host. Unless you have a clear roadmap from hybrid to something more fundamentally modern, lift-and-shift can become a comfortable trap that nobody wants to name out loud.

Comparison: Control, Cost, Speed, and Compliance

Dimension Cloud-Native Rebuild SaaS Platform Hybrid Lift-and-Shift
Control Full – you own architecture and data model Limited – vendor controls platform and upgrade schedule High – existing logic unchanged, new infra layer only
Upfront Cost Very high (8-figure range for mid-size carriers) Moderate upfront; recurring subscription scales with book Lower initial cost; ongoing infra savings vs. on-prem
Time to Value 2-4 years to production at scale 12-18 months for defined LOB 3-9 months to cloud; years to actual modernization
Regulatory Compliance Built by you; requires your own audit trail Largely inherited from vendor certifications Unchanged from current state; compliance posture doesn’t improve automatically
Scalability Excellent once mature Good; vendor-managed elasticity Better than on-prem; still limited by legacy app design
Talent Requirements Cloud engineers, architects, DevOps – competitive market Vendor-specific configuration skills; smaller team Existing team can manage; some cloud upskilling needed

Source: Framework informed by KPMG Insurance Technology Survey 2026 and AWS insurance industry benchmark data. Individual carrier results will vary based on book size, product complexity, and existing infrastructure.

Scenario-Based Recommendations

You’re a Regional Carrier With a Concentrated Book in 2-3 States

SaaS is probably your best path. Your regulatory exposure is manageable, the vendor’s compliance library will cover most of what you need, and you likely don’t have the IT org to sustain a multi-year cloud-native build. Pick a platform with demonstrated strength in your lines – personal auto, homeowners, commercial package, whatever your focus is – and invest heavily in implementation partner selection, because that’s where regional carriers usually lose the most time. Not in the technology. In the partner.

You’re a Large National Carrier With Complex, Proprietary Products

A SaaS platform might constrain you more than it helps. If your competitive advantage lives in product structures that don’t map cleanly to standard data models, you need more control than most insurance policy admin systems in the SaaS category actually allow. Cloud-native rebuild is the right long-term answer here, but consider a phased approach: move a simpler line of business first, prove the architecture, then migrate complexity. Don’t try to rebuild everything at once. That’s how these projects stall out.

You Need to Modernize But Can’t Absorb a Multi-Year Disruption

Hybrid lift-and-shift, done deliberately, can be a legitimate bridge. Move your policy administration systems to IaaS, stabilize operations, and use the breathing room to plan the deeper transformation properly. Just be honest with your board that this is step one of two, not the finish line. The mainframe to cloud migration gets you on better infrastructure. It doesn’t get you a modern system. Those are different things.

You’re a Startup or Greenfield MGA

Cloud-native from day one. You have no legacy constraints, and the SaaS platforms weren’t really designed for the highly specialized or non-standard product structures that many MGAs operate in. Build an API-first insurance policy management system, keep your core logic modular, and resist the temptation to add complexity early just because you can. You’ll regret it later if you don’t.

What KPMG and AWS Data Actually Tell Us

The KPMG Insurance Technology Survey 2026 flags something worth taking seriously: carriers that attempt core modernization without executive-level ownership of the program fail at a significantly higher rate than those where a C-suite sponsor is actively involved. Technology decisions get made in vendor meetings. Transformation decisions get made in the boardroom. If your policy administration modernization is being run exclusively at the CIO level without CFO and COO alignment on trade-offs, that’s a risk factor regardless of which delivery model you choose.

AWS insurance industry benchmark data on migration timelines is a bit more optimistic than our experience suggests is typical, particularly for carriers with complex state filings and multi-line books. The benchmark cases tend to skew toward simpler lines with cleaner data. If your policy administration environment has decades of mid-policy endorsements, manual overrides, and undocumented business rules baked into production – and most do – add 20-30% to any vendor-provided timeline estimate. That’s not pessimism. That’s calibration.

FAQ

How do we know if our current policy administration system qualifies as “legacy”?

Generally, if your system was implemented before 2005, runs on a mainframe or end-of-life hardware, requires significant manual workarounds for new product launches, or can’t expose data via APIs without a middleware translation layer, it’s legacy by any practical definition. Age alone isn’t the issue. The inability to adapt to market and regulatory demands is. Those are related but not the same thing.

Can we run SaaS and a legacy system in parallel during transition?

Yes, and most carriers do. The dual-run period is normal and expected. The critical decisions are around which system is the system of record for new business versus in-force policies, how you handle renewals that span the cutover date, and how long you’re willing to fund both environments simultaneously. We’ve seen parallel runs stretch to five years when those decisions aren’t made up front. Define your exit criteria before you start, not six months in when everyone’s exhausted.

What’s the biggest regulatory risk specific to insurance policy admin modernization?

State-by-state filing requirements are the most common trap. Different states have different rules about rate and form filings, data residency, and audit trail requirements. According to NAIC cloud computing guidance, insurers are expected to maintain data integrity and auditability regardless of where systems are hosted. A cloud-native rebuild gives you maximum control over compliance architecture but requires you to build it yourself. SaaS platforms vary significantly in how much regulatory content they include out of the box – ask vendors specifically about your states and lines before signing. Don’t assume it’s covered.

Where to Land

There’s a version of this decision where you pick the model that looks best on a slide and spend three years discovering why it didn’t fit your actual organization. We’d rather you start from constraints: What’s your realistic IT capacity? What’s your board’s actual tolerance for a multi-year disruption? Do your products fit standard data models, or are they genuinely differentiated in ways that matter competitively?

The delivery model follows from honest answers to those questions, not the other way around. If you want to pressure-test your current thinking against your specific book, product mix, and regulatory footprint, that’s exactly the kind of conversation worth having before you’re two years into a rebuild that’s running 18 months behind schedule and burning through budget faster than anyone projected.
